draft.title: Metallic bonding
card: A metal is a lattice of positive metal ions. The outer electrons leave their atoms and move freely between the ions. These are delocalised electrons, often called a sea of electrons.
Metallic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons. It is strong, so metals have high melting points.
The electrons are free to move, so they carry electric charge and pass on heat energy. This is why metals conduct electricity and heat.

Layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking the bonding, because the electrons still surround the ions. This makes metals malleable, which means they can be hammered into shape without breaking. The electrons also reflect light, which gives metals their lustre.
draft.remember: Positive ions in a sea of moving electrons: the attraction holds the metal together, and the free electrons carry charge and heat.

a.q: Which feature of metallic bonding explains why copper conducts electricity?
opts: Delocalised electrons that are free to move
Positive ions that are free to move
Electrons held tightly between two atoms
Neutral atoms that are free to move
a.why: Delocalised electrons move through the lattice and carry charge. The ions stay in fixed positions in the lattice, so they do not carry the current in a solid metal.
a.clue: What moves in a solid metal to carry charge?

b.q: Hana hammers a sheet of silver into a thin shape and it does not shatter. Which statement best explains this?
opts: Layers of ions slide while the electrons keep bonding them
Layers of ions slide and the bonding between them breaks
The ions are replaced by neutral atoms as it is hammered
The electrons are pushed out of the metal as it is hammered
b.why: When the layers slide, the delocalised electrons still surround the ions, so the attraction remains and the metal stays in one piece. The idea that the bonding breaks is tempting, but breaking bonds would make the metal crack.
b.clue: After the layers slide, what still surrounds the ions?

a.best: Delocalised electrons that are free to move

b.best: Layers of ions slide while the electrons keep bonding them

problems.detail: The card says metals have high melting points without a qualifier such as 'most' or 'generally'. Some metals have low melting points: mercury is a liquid at room temperature, and sodium and potassium melt below 100 °C. Saying 'most metals have high melting points' would be accurate.
